title: A census map of one country: scale, pattern and limits

readings.title: Homes with piped water by province, Country A, 2020 census (invented)

parts.label: A
parts.demand: Give the information asked for: a word or short phrase can earn the point, with no reasons needed.
parts.prompt: Identify the scale of analysis of the data shown on the map.

rubric.point: Names the local (subnational or provincial) scale.

parts.sample: The local (subnational) scale: there is one value for each province.

parts.label: B
parts.demand: Give the relevant characteristics: what it is like, where and how much. A name alone earns nothing.
parts.prompt: Describe the pattern of homes with piped water shown on the map.

rubric.point: Describes where shares are high and low with named provinces from the map.
accept: highest in the Capital Region and Lake District, lowest in the Western Uplands and Southern Forest
high in the center and northeast, low in the west and south

parts.sample: The share of homes with piped water is highest, 80% or more, in the Capital Region and the Lake District, and lowest, under 40%, in the Western Uplands and the Southern Forest.

parts.label: C
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain one reason why the share of homes with piped water could be higher in the Capital Region than in the Western Uplands.

rubric.point: Gives a reason with its link, such as more people and money close together, so pipes reach more homes at lower cost.
accept: many homes packed close together, so each kilometer of pipe serves more homes
the capital has more government money and services, so networks were built there first
steep, high land in the uplands makes pipes costly, so fewer were built

parts.sample: In the Capital Region many homes are close together, so each kilometer of pipe serves many households, which makes building a network cheaper than in the scattered villages of the Western Uplands.

parts.label: D
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain how the national government of Country A could use these census data to make a decision.

rubric.point: Names a decision and links it to what the data show.
accept: send money for new pipes to the provinces under 40%, because the map shows where need is greatest
set priorities for water projects by province, so funds go where access is lowest

parts.sample: The government could send most of its water budget to the Western Uplands and Southern Forest, because the census shows fewer than 40% of homes there have piped water, so new pipes would reach the most homes in need.

parts.label: E
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain one limitation of census data such as these for planning water projects.

rubric.point: Names a limitation and why it matters for planning.
accept: the census is from 2020, so homes built since then are missing
some people are undercounted, so needs may be larger than shown
one value per province hides villages that differ, so projects may miss them

parts.sample: The census was taken in 2020, so it misses homes built since then, which means new neighborhoods without pipes may not appear in the data.

parts.label: F
parts.demand: Give a similarity or a difference and say it about both things, not one.
parts.prompt: Compare what this map shows with what one national figure for piped water in Country A would show.

rubric.point: Speaks of both: the map shows differences between provinces, whereas a national figure gives one average that hides them.
accept: the map shows a gap between provinces, while a national figure hides it
both use the same census, but one is aggregated

parts.sample: The map shows that access ranges from under 40% in the Western Uplands to 80% or more in the Capital Region, whereas one national figure would give a single average that hides those differences.

parts.label: G
parts.demand: State the degree first (to a high, moderate or low degree), then explain why with evidence.
parts.prompt: Explain the degree to which this map could be used to decide which villages within the Western Uplands need new water pipes.

rubric.point: States a degree first, then explains that province data cannot show villages inside a province.
accept: low degree: one value for the whole province, so it cannot show which villages lack pipes
small extent: it shows the province needs help but not where within it

parts.sample: To a low degree: the map gives one value for the whole Western Uplands, so it shows the province needs pipes but cannot show which villages inside it lack them; village-level data would be needed.
